```{r setup}
#| cache: false
# The connection can't be cached, so this chunk always re-runs.
library(duckdb)   # query engine; runs inside R and reads files over the web
library(DBI)      # connects R to the engine
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)  # name cleaning in the EIA crosswalk
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Only open a connection if there is not a live one, so this is safe to re-run.
if (!exists("con") || !dbIsValid(con)) {
  con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
  invisible(dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs;"))
  invisible(dbExecute(con, "LOAD httpfs;"))
  invisible(dbExecute(con, "SET memory_limit='4GB';"))
  invisible(dbExecute(con, "SET preserve_insertion_order=false;"))
}

# PUDL publishes one Parquet file per EQR table per quarter at this address.
BASE <- "https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/pudl.catalyst.coop/ferceqr"
eqr  <- function(tb, yq) sprintf("%s/%s/%s.parquet", BASE, tb, yq)

# PUDL's other datasets, including EIA, are not partitioned: one file per table.
PUDL <- "https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/pudl.catalyst.coop/stable"
pudl <- function(tb) sprintf("%s/%s.parquet", PUDL, tb)

# Several file addresses as a SQL list: c("a","b") -> ['a','b']
flist <- function(urls) paste0("['", paste(urls, collapse = "','"), "']")

# All 52 quarters, 2013 Q3 to 2026 Q2.
ALL_Q <- c("2013q3", "2013q4",
           paste0(rep(2014:2025, each = 4), "q", 1:4),
           "2026q1", "2026q2")

# Every quarter of contracts, as one list for read_parquet().
all_c <- flist(eqr("core_ferceqr__contracts", ALL_Q))

TABLES <- c("core_ferceqr__contracts", "core_ferceqr__transactions",
            "core_ferceqr__quarterly_identity", "core_ferceqr__quarterly_index_pub")

EX_Q  <- "2024q1"   # the quarter used for every single-quarter example
c_url <- eqr("core_ferceqr__contracts",    EX_Q)
t_url <- eqr("core_ferceqr__transactions", EX_Q)
```


# Introduction: A Dataset Nobody Can Use

If you want to know what wholesale electricity costs in a place like
Pennsylvania or California, the answer is easy to find. Regional grid operators
like PJM and CAISO run auctions a day ahead and again in real time, and they
publish the clearing price for every location on their system, down to
five-minute intervals. Researchers have been using these prices for over twenty
years. About two thirds of U.S. electricity load is served in regions with one
of these organized markets [@ferc2024primer, p. 37].

However, a public spot price does not mean most power is actually bought at that
price. Even in PJM, the largest of these markets, the independent market monitor
found that only 25.2 percent of real-time load in 2019 was bought on the spot
market. Another 15.9 percent came through bilateral contracts, and the remaining
58.9 percent was self-supply, meaning utilities serving their customers from
generation they own [@pjm2019som].

Outside the organized markets, even less is visible. In the Southeast and most
of the West outside California, utilities usually own their generation,
transmission and distribution together, and FERC's handbook says that there
"wholesale physical power trading typically occurs through bilateral
transactions" [@ferc2024primer, p. 60]. These regions do have some market
structures, but they are narrow. The Western Energy Imbalance Market, which
CAISO has run since 2014, only balances supply and demand in real time, and FERC
estimates it handles "about two to three percent of the energy used to meet load
in the participating" areas [@ferc2024primer, pp. 62, 98]. The Southeast Energy
Exchange Market launched in November 2022 and was sent back to FERC by the D.C.
Circuit the following July [@ferc2024primer, p. 62]. Neither one commits power
plants, buys capacity, or replaces the contracts that utilities in those regions
actually use to buy power. This is starting to change in the West, where CAISO's
Extended Day-Ahead Market went live with PacifiCorp on May 1, 2026
[@caiso2026edam], but for the period this dataset covers the description above
holds.

In plain terms, the part of the market we can see is the spot price, and the
part we mostly cannot see is the contracts and self-supply arrangements behind
the majority of what is bought and sold.

**Why the contracts matter.** Contracts are not just a different way to buy the
same power. They are also how new power plants get built. A developer with a
signed agreement to sell its output for ten or twenty years can show a lender a
predictable revenue stream, and FERC's handbook makes this link when it says
market participants hedge to establish "a predictable cash flow to support
financing" [@ferc2024primer, p. 129]. This means that even where spot prices
are public, without contract data we have limited visibility into how new firms
enter wholesale electricity markets, who they sell to, and on what terms.
**[CHECK]** Maybe find a second source for the financing claim beyond the Primer.

**Why economists care.** This gap matters for at least three areas in
economics. The first is the study on market efficiency and restructuring,
which asks whether moving from regulated monopolies to competitive markets
lowered costs [@fabrizio2007markets] and whether organized markets use power
plants more efficiently than bilateral trading [@mansur2012market;
@cicala2022imperfect]. The second is the study on long-term contracting.
Joskow's study of coal contracts found that contracts last longer when the buyer
and seller have more invested in the relationship [@joskow1987contract]. In
electricity specifically, forward contracts change how firms behave in the spot
market, since a firm that has already sold most of its output in advance has
less reason to push prices up [@allaz1993cournot; @bushnell2008vertical]. The
third is the industrial organization study on bargaining between firms,
which estimates how negotiated prices depend on what each side could get
elsewhere [@crawford2012welfare; @grennan2013price]. Bilateral power contracts
are a natural setting for that kind of model, but only if you can see the
contracts. **[TODO]** I have only read Borenstein and Bushnell and Bushnell,
Mansur and Saravia very closely. Read more of the others before
confirming them. **[ADVISOR]** Are there better examples for the bargaining
literature, or electricity-specific ones? Or other areas I am missing?

## The data exists

What surprised me is that these contracts are not private at all.

Since 2002, and in its current form since the third quarter of 2013, every
company selling wholesale electricity under federal jurisdiction has had to
report its contracts and its individual sales to FERC four times a year, on Form
No. 920, the Electric Quarterly Report (EQR) [@ferc2023filing]. The filings name
the seller, name the buyer, describe the product, and give the price.

The requirement also reaches further than I first expected. A "public utility"
under the Federal Power Act is "any person who owns or operates facilities
subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission," and those facilities can be
"paper facilities, e.g., contracts, books & records" [@greenfield2018ferc101,
slide 13]. So a trading company that owns no wires and no power plants is still
a public utility, and it still files.

To be specific about what is new: none of this data is new. FERC has published
the filings on its own website the whole time. What changed in 2026 is not
whether the data is public, but how hard it is to use.

## So why has it been used so little?

The short answer is the format. FERC distributes the EQR as zip archives inside
zip archives of CSV files, which PUDL describes as "hundreds of gigabytes of
nested zip files" [@lamb2026eqr]. The schema also changed across three versions
of the data dictionary over the decade [@ferc2014dictionary;
@ferc2017dictionary; @ferc2020dictionary], some archives are corrupt, and
character encodings are inconsistent. Pulling one quarter was a small project.
Pulling the full history and getting it into one consistent shape was more work
than most researchers would take on for a dataset they could not look at first.

That does not mean nobody used it. Commercial data vendors sell processed
versions of the EQR to industry clients [@yesenergy2026eqr], so the barrier
fell mostly on researchers and the public, who had to either pay or build the
pipeline themselves. A small number of academic papers have built it. Andonov
and Rauh, for example, combine EQR contracts with EIA plant data to study how
new types of power plant owners, like private equity, contract differently from
traditional utilities [@andonov2024shifting].

More often, researchers have either worked around the EQR or used it by hand.
Cicala is a good example of working around it. To compare bilateral trading with
organized markets, he builds supply and demand curves for areas without a market
from power plant production and fuel data, mainly EIA Form 923, instead of from
contract prices [@cicala2022imperfect]. His method has since been used in other
papers, and it shows how much can be learned without the EQR. But it estimates
what trading should have looked like from plant costs. It does not observe the
prices firms actually agreed to.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory is the main example of using it by hand.
Their annual report on utility-scale solar is the standard reference for solar
power purchase agreement (PPA) prices in the U.S., and the EQR is one of its main
sources for those prices. The 2025 edition reports 546 solar PPAs since 2007,
41 of them for 2024 [@lbnl2025solar].

Overall, the data was public and people clearly wanted it, but using it at
scale was out of reach for most researchers.

In February 2026 that changed. The Public Utility Data Liberation project
(PUDL), run by the nonprofit Catalyst Cooperative, released a processed version
of the EQR: the same filings from 2013 Q3 on, extracted, given one consistent
schema, and published as Apache Parquet files in public cloud storage, one file
per table per quarter [@pudl2026ferceqr; @lamb2026eqr]. This release is what
makes this project possible, and it is the reason the dataset is getting new
attention now.

## What PUDL changed, and what is still in the way

PUDL calls its release a "minimally transformed version" of the data
[@lamb2026eqr], and that is accurate: it fixes the format, but it does not try
to fix the content. Section 3 describes exactly what changed.

PUDL also published a field catalog: every column, its type, and a description,
mostly copied from FERC's instructions to filers [@pudl2026dictionary]. It tells
you a column exists. It does not tell you what a row represents, and in this
data that matters more than you would expect. The table named `contracts` does
not have one row per contract. A contract gets re-reported in every quarter it
stays active, and within a single quarter it takes a separate row for each
customer, each product, and each distinct rate. In 2024 Q1 the table has 199,603
rows but only 57,359 distinct contracts. So someone who counts rows is off by a
factor of about three and a half, and nothing in the output tells them.

This turned out to be a pattern rather than a one-off. A field called
`contact_state` looks like geography, but it is the filer's mailing address,
which is why Texas ranks first on it even though most of Texas is exempt from
filing. A third of contracts have no term recorded, which looks like missing
data but is mostly filers correctly reporting that no term applies, with that
distinction lost in cleaning. And a categorical field that looks stable across
the decade quietly splits into sixteen values in 2021.

None of these problems cause an error. The query runs and the number looks
reasonable. The hard part is figuring out whether it means what the column name
says, and that is why I decided to write a guide rather than a single analysis.

## What this project does

This project does four main things:

First, it describes the dataset: what FERC collects and from whom, what the
four tables contain, what a row means in each, and which variables have enough
information to use.

Second, it documents a computational method. The data is bigger than my laptop's
memory and bigger than its disk, so the usual approach of downloading a file and
opening it does not work. I never downloaded anything. Section 4 covers how to
query the files where they sit, aggregate remotely, and pull down only the
result.

Third, it works through one or two real questions from the first query to a
defensible answer, including the checks that decide whether the answer holds.
The focus is on getting reliable estimates of basic contract characteristics,
like how long contracts last or how many buyers a seller has, because every
more ambitious question depends on getting those right first.

Fourth (not finalizied), it includes a dashboard for exploring contract trends without writing
code (Section 7).

It also reports what I could not do. Buyers appear only as free text with no
identifier, so following one buyer across the decade is still an open problem,
and contract duration cannot be measured because most contracts have no
termination date recorded. Both are in Section 9 rather than buried.

## Who this is for

The first audience I have in mind is a researcher or analyst who wants to use this data and has not seen it before. For this reader, writing the query is an initial learning curve, but can be assisted with AI or reading included SQL chunks. The harder part is knowing
what the rows mean, which fields can be trusted, and which obvious queries give
the wrong answer. That is where most of this guide spends its time. I assume no
energy background and build what is needed in Section 2.

The second audience is policymakers, industry analysts and the general public,
who mostly want to see trends without writing any code. This is a larger group
than academic economists, and the dashboard in Section 7 is built for them.

The guide is also written for whoever opens this dataset next.

## How this is organized

Section 2 explains how wholesale electricity gets bought and sold. Section 3
describes the dataset: who files, who is exempt, what the four tables hold, and
what a row means. Section 4 covers the computational method. Section 5 reports
what I found when I checked the data instead of trusting it. Section 6 works
through the examples. Section 7 describes the interactive tool. Section 8 takes
up ethical questions. Section 9 sets out limitations and next steps.

# Background: How Wholesale Electricity Gets Bought and Sold

This section covers the vocabulary needed to read the rest of the paper.
Readers with an energy background can skip to Section 3.

**Wholesale is not retail.** The bill you pay at home is retail, and retail is
not what this dataset records. Before power reaches a household it is usually
bought at least once at wholesale, between companies. FERC puts it this way:
"Retail service involves the sales of electricity to consumers and may involve
retail markets; wholesale markets typically involve the sales of electricity
among electric utilities and electricity traders before it is eventually sold
to consumers" [@ferc2024primer, p. 33]. FERC regulates wholesale rates and not
retail ones, and that is the whole reason this dataset exists.

**A few units.** *Load* is the total demand for electricity on the grid at a
given moment. A *megawatt* (MW) measures a rate, how much power is flowing or
could flow right now. A *megawatt-hour* (MWh) measures an amount, one megawatt
sustained for one hour. Energy is sold in MWh and capacity in MW, and the
dataset uses both.

**Who the players are.** On the selling side are investor-owned utilities,
independent generators, trading companies that buy power and resell it, and
some public entities like the Bonneville Power Administration (Section 3
explains why a federal agency files). On the buying side are load-serving
entities, meaning the companies responsible for actually supplying customers.
FERC describes their three options directly: a load-serving entity serves its
customers "through a combination of self-supply, bilateral market purchases and
purchases from RTO/ISO markets" [@ferc2024primer, p. 53]. Self-supply means
generating the power yourself. The other two are where this dataset lives.
Buyers and sellers are sometimes *affiliates*, meaning they are owned by the
same parent company, and the dataset flags these contracts.

**Two structures, not two markets.** The United States is split into two
arrangements. In roughly two thirds of the country by load, a regional
transmission organization or independent system operator (RTO/ISO) runs
centralized auctions: generators offer, buyers bid, and the market clears at a
published price, first in a *day-ahead* market that schedules the next day and
then in a *real-time* market that settles the differences as the day happens
[@ferc2024primer, pp. 37, 66]. There are seven RTO/ISOs, and FERC regulates all
of them except ERCOT in Texas [@ferc2024primer, p. 66]. In the rest of the
country, utilities are typically vertically integrated, meaning they own
generation, transmission and distribution together, and trading happens
bilaterally [@ferc2024primer, p. 60]. In both structures, the grid is divided
into *balancing authority areas*, each run by an entity responsible for keeping
supply and demand matched in real time. Balancing authorities matter here
because they are the closest thing to a location the dataset records.

The important thing, and the one I had wrong at first, is that these are not
alternatives. Bilateral contracting happens inside the organized markets too
[@ferc2024primer, p. 53]. An RTO changes how power is dispatched and priced in
the short run. It does not replace the agreements underneath.

**What restructuring was.** The split above came out of a specific period.
Before the 1990s most customers were served by a regulated, vertically
integrated monopoly that did everything and recovered its costs through
regulated rates. Between 1995 and 2002, a wave of state-level reforms separated
those functions in many states [@borenstein2015restructuring, p. 1]. The share
of U.S. electricity produced by independent power producers went from 1.6
percent in 1997 to about 35 percent in 2012 [@borenstein2015restructuring,
pp. 5-6]. The movement stopped after the California electricity crisis of
2000-2001, and Borenstein and Bushnell describe policy since then as a halt
rather than a reversal [@borenstein2015restructuring, p. 1].

**Market-based and cost-based rates.** Even fully restructured wholesale
markets are still regulated by FERC. Borenstein and Bushnell note that FERC "has
applied its authority flexibly by allowing states and regions to set
'market-based' rates," but "such authority can be revoked, however, so it is
inaccurate to label even wholesale markets in fully restructured regions as
'deregulated'" [@borenstein2015restructuring, p. 2]. In practice there are two
kinds of sellers. A seller with *cost-based* rates charges prices FERC has
approved based on its costs, the traditional way utilities were regulated. A
seller with *market-based rate authority* can negotiate its own prices, which
FERC allows once it finds the seller does not have market power. The EQR is part
of the price of that freedom: it is how FERC keeps watching sellers it no longer
sets prices for. The dataset records which kind of rate each contract falls
under. **[CHECK]** Cite FERC's market-based rate program page and Order No. 2001
for the link between market-based rates and EQR reporting.

**What is actually sold.** Several distinct things, and the dataset tells them
apart.

*Energy* is electricity delivered, measured in megawatt-hours. *Capacity* is the
commitment to be available, measured in megawatts, and it is bought separately
because a system needs more generating capability than it uses on a normal day
[@ferc2024primer, p. 72]. *Ancillary services* are the smaller products that
keep the grid stable: regulation, which follows second-to-second changes in
load; spinning reserve, which is generation already running and able to ramp up
within about ten minutes; and reactive supply, which maintains voltage
[@ferc2024primer, p. 58].

*Transmission* is the right to move power over someone else's wires. Generating
power and delivering it are separate businesses, so a buyer often contracts
separately for transport. Two forms show up in this data. *Network service*
allows use of the whole transmission system to move generation to specified
loads. *Point-to-point service* reserves a fixed quantity between a point of
receipt and a point of delivery, and can run "for durations of one hour to
multiple years" [@ferc2024primer, p. 55]. Point of receipt and point of
delivery are both column names in the dataset.

*Firm* and *non-firm* describe how reliably the product arrives. Firm service
commits the seller and cannot be interrupted for economic reasons. Non-firm is
as-available, and FERC's data dictionary describes it as delivery that "may be
interrupted for any reason or no reason, without liability on the part of either
the buyer or seller" [@ferc2020dictionary]. Firm costs more, because the seller
is holding capability in reserve. A third category, *unit power sale*, ties the
delivery to specific named power plants rather than to the seller's whole
fleet. The Energy Primer uses "firm" for electricity without defining it, so I
take these definitions from the EQR data dictionary, which is also where the
codes in the dataset come from.

**How a deal is structured.** Bilateral power deals usually have two layers. The
industry standard is the Edison Electric Institute Master Power Purchase and Sale
Agreement, under which parties "may make a bilateral sale by agreeing to
transaction-specific values for price, quantity, delivery location, and period
of delivery," with "the terms of the transaction documented on a
transaction-specific confirmation" [@ferc2024primer, p. 123]. So there is a
master agreement, and then individual confirmations under it. This lines up
with the EQR having a contracts table and a transactions table, and it is the
clearest explanation I found of why the data is shaped the way it is.

more with her to make sure nothing is missing or overstated.

# The Data: FERC's Electric Quarterly Reports

## What the EQR is

Every company that sells wholesale electricity under federal jurisdiction has
to tell FERC what it sold, to whom, and on what terms, and it does this four
times a year on FERC Form No. 920, the Electric Quarterly Report. The
requirement dates to 2002 and the filing regime in its current form began in
the third quarter of 2013, which is where the data available through PUDL
starts.

One detail about the filing obligation shapes everything downstream: it does
not depend on activity. A utility with a tariff on file has to submit a report
even if it made no sales at all that quarter [@ferc2023filing, p. 7]. The
population of filers is therefore wider than the population of sellers, and
any count of companies in this dataset is counting the former rather than the
latter.

**Who is left out.** Three exclusions shape what questions the data can
answer, and all three are worth knowing before you start rather than after.
Utilities located entirely in Alaska or Hawaii are exempt because they are not
electrically connected to the contiguous grid. Non-public utilities, mainly
cooperatives and public power agencies, file only if their wholesale sales
exceed four million megawatt-hours a year, and sales to their own members do
not count toward that threshold [@cfr35].

The third exclusion is ERCOT, which covers most of Texas, and it is the one
that limits this dataset most. The reason is the same electrical isolation
that exempts Alaska and Hawaii, since ERCOT is not synchronously interconnected
with the rest of the country, so most sales inside it never enter interstate
commerce in the legal sense. That distinction is worth stating carefully,
because the intuitive version of the rule is wrong. Being intrastate is not by
itself enough to escape FERC jurisdiction, since interstate commerce has been
read to cover a transaction even when the contracting parties and the
electrical pathway between them sit within one state, as long as the system is
interconnected with the interstate grid [@greenfield2018ferc101, slide 15]. The
exemption turns on electrical isolation, not on geography.

However, ERCOT is not quite fully absent, and I want to be precise about this because an
earlier draft of mine said it was. A small number of contracts do record an
ERCOT delivery point, presumably the limited exceptions that FERC's own
summary hedges about. But against a market the size of Texas, which is among
the largest wind and solar markets in the country, that is a rounding error,
and anyone who needs ERCOT has to use ERCOT's own published data instead.

## Filings get revised

Filed data is not final when it is submitted. A seller must revise a quarter by
the end of the following quarter, and must correct errors going back twelve
quarters [@ferc2023filing, pp. 26-27]. FERC is direct about why, noting that
many filers "do not have complete, final data for the full quarter by the EQR
filing deadlines," particularly for sales to ISOs [@ferc2002order2001, para. 9].

Nothing in the published data marks a row as revised, so a number pulled today
may not match the same number pulled next year and there is no way to tell from
the files which quarters moved. I spent some time treating this as a
theoretical concern and then it happened to me. When I first wrote this section
in October, the 2024 Q1 contracts file held 199,603 rows and the transactions
file held 143,323,121. Re-running the identical query six weeks later returned
199,278 and 143,442,727. Contracts lost 325 rows and transactions gained
119,606, in a quarter that had closed two years earlier.

That is a small drift in percentage terms and it is also exactly the problem.
Nothing failed, nothing warned me, and the only reason I noticed is that I
happened to have the old numbers written down. For a guide whose examples are
supposed to be re-runnable, the practical response is to pin and report a
retrieval date rather than to pretend the numbers are stable, and that is what
I do from here on. Every figure in this thesis comes from a single render, and
the date of that render is stated on the title page.

## The four tables

PUDL distributes the cleaned data as four tables, stored as one Parquet file
per table per quarter. Table 1 gives the shape of each in a single quarter.

```{r tbl-inventory}
inventory <- lapply(TABLES, function(tb) {
  url  <- eqr(tb, EX_Q)
  cols <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
    "DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('%s')", url))
  rows <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
    "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM read_parquet('%s')", url))
  data.frame(Table   = sub("core_ferceqr__", "", tb),
             Columns = nrow(cols),
             Rows    = rows$n)
})
inventory <- do.call(rbind, inventory)

inventory |>
  mutate(Rows = format(Rows, big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable(caption = "Shape of each EQR table in 2024 Q1. Both the column count and the row count come from each Parquet file's footer rather than from its contents, so this table is quick to produce even though the transactions file is roughly 1.5 GB.")
```

Two of these carry the substance. `contracts` describes agreements and
`transactions` records what was actually sold under them.
`quarterly_identity` is a directory of who filed and how to reach them, and
`quarterly_index_pub` records which filers report to commercial price indices,
which is a table with a limited future given the rule change discussed in
Section 9.

The size gap between contracts and transactions is the single most important
practical fact about this dataset. One quarter of transactions is over seven
hundred times the size of one quarter of contracts, and Section 4 is largely
about how to work with a table that size without downloading it.

## What a row means

This is the part that took me longest to get right, and as far as I can tell it
is not written down anywhere. The two main tables have different units of
observation, and in neither case is it the one the table name suggests.

**A transaction row is one sale, but sales are reported very finely.** FERC
requires a new record every time the price changes, and prices "cannot be
averaged or otherwise aggregated" before filing [@ferc2023filing, p. 26]. For a
seller settling in an organized market that means a new row every five minutes,
which is why one quarter runs to
`r format(inventory$Rows[inventory$Table == "transactions"], big.mark = ",")`
rows. Section 5 puts a number on how small the typical row is, and it is
smaller than I expected.

**A contract row is not a contract.** It is one line of one contract as
reported in one quarter, and two separate mechanisms multiply the rows.

The first is restatement. A contract is reported from the quarter service
begins and keeps being reported "until they are terminated"
[@ferc2023filing, p. 16]. FERC considered the alternative and rejected it
explicitly, writing that "we reject Edison Mission's suggestion that contract
data should be reported only in the quarter when the agreement is entered"
[@ferc2002order2001, para. 216]. A five-year agreement therefore appears in
twenty consecutive quarterly files.

The second is line splitting. Within a single quarter, one agreement occupies
several rows whenever it has multiple customers, multiple products, multiple
rates, or a quantity that changes over its life. FERC's own illustration is a
five-year contract with a different price each year, in which "the product
(power) would be listed on five lines" [@ferc2023filing, p. 48].

The consequence is that counting rows in the contracts table does not count
contracts, and the error is not small. The two mechanisms compound, so a long
agreement with several products gets counted once per product per quarter it
stays alive.

What works instead is counting distinct contracts, keyed on the seller's FERC
company ID together with the service agreement ID the seller assigned. This is
what FERC intends the agreement ID to be used for, describing it as serving
"the dual purpose of being a unique method for identifying a particular
contract when it is requested and a means of tracking a contract and the
activity under a contract from quarter to quarter" [@ferc2002order2001,
Order No. 2001-G, para. 21]. The seller ID has to come along with it, because
nothing stops two sellers from both numbering an agreement `1`, and in practice
many do.

```{r tbl-rows-vs-contracts}
# concat_ws rather than || is deliberate. About 2% of contract rows have no
# seller ID, and || returns NULL if either side is NULL, which silently drops
# those rows from count(DISTINCT). Section 5 shows what that costs.
row_vs_contract <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT count(*) AS rows_in_table,
         count(DISTINCT concat_ws('|',
                 CAST(seller_company_id_ferc AS VARCHAR),
                 contract_service_agreement_id)) AS distinct_contracts
    FROM read_parquet('%s')", c_url))

tibble::tibble(
  Measure = c("Rows in the table", "Distinct contracts", "Ratio"),
  Value   = c(format(row_vs_contract$rows_in_table,      big.mark = ","),
              format(row_vs_contract$distinct_contracts, big.mark = ","),
              sprintf("%.1f rows per contract",
                      row_vs_contract$rows_in_table /
                      row_vs_contract$distinct_contracts))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Rows versus contracts in the 2024 Q1 contracts table. The gap here is line splitting alone, since within a single quarter each contract is restated exactly once.")
```

The ratio in Table 2 reflects only line splitting, because within one quarter
each contract appears exactly once in restatement terms. Across the full
history the two effects compound, and Section 5 shows what that looks like by
stacking three quarters and measuring the duplication directly.

One note on how that query is written. I build the key with `concat_ws` rather
than with SQL's `||` operator, which is the more obvious choice. `||` returns
NULL whenever either input is NULL, and roughly two percent of contract rows
have no seller company ID, so the obvious version silently discards those rows
and returns a smaller count with no warning. Section 5 measures exactly how
many contracts that loses. I mention it here because the composite key is
introduced here, and anyone copying this query should copy the right version
of it.

## Linking contracts to transactions

The obvious question is whether you can take a contract and find the sales made
under it, and for a long time I assumed the answer was no. FERC's filing
requirements say that four fields must match across the two tables: seller
company name, customer company name, FERC tariff reference, and contract
service agreement ID [@ferc2023filing, pp. 50-51]. PUDL, however, warns that
the company name fields are unreliable and recommends joining on company ID
instead, and their own characterization of the contracts table concluded that
it "does not appear to have a primary key or an easy way to link it to the
transactions table" [@pudlissues, issue 4513]. Given that the people who built
the cleaned dataset had looked at this and come away without a key, I did not
expect to find one.

There was also an asymmetry in PUDL's notes that I did not understand at first.
They report that 94 to 97 percent of seller-buyer pairs appearing in
transactions also appear in contracts, but that only about 25 percent of pairs
in contracts appear in transactions. Most contracts, in other words, generate
no recorded sales in a given quarter. That is not necessarily an error, and
FERC's rules guarantee some of it, since transmission and interconnection
agreements are contract-only products with no transaction counterpart at all
[@ferc2023filing, p. 60], and any agreement that is signed but not drawn on in
a quarter will sit in the contracts table with nothing beside it.

The join does work, and Section 6 tests it in full. The short version is that
the contract service agreement ID is populated on every one of the 143 million
transaction rows in 2024 Q1, and that joining on the seller's FERC company ID,
the agreement ID and the product name matches 99.9 percent of those rows to a
contract filed in the same quarter. The agreement ID alone is not enough, for
the reason given above. The seller and agreement ID together are still not
quite enough, because of line splitting. Adding the product is what resolves
it, since a contract row is split by product and a transaction records which
product it was. Looked at from the other direction, about 18 percent of the
quarter's contracts show any transaction activity, which sits close enough to
the 25 percent PUDL reported that I take their asymmetry to be a real feature
of the data rather than a symptom of a bad join.

Two things about that result belong here rather than in Section 6. The first is
that the key I use is not the key FERC documents, since I never use customer
company name or tariff reference and I do use product name, which FERC's
four-field list does not mention. A looser key is easier to satisfy, so a high
match rate on its own would not prove much, which is why Section 6 validates
the join against contracted prices rather than stopping at the match rate. The
second is that everything here comes from one quarter, and until the same test
has been run on an earlier one I would describe this as a result for 2024 Q1
rather than as a property of the dataset.

## Which variables carry information

A table with `r nrow(dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('%s')", c_url)))`
columns does not have that many usable variables. Some are populated in nearly
every row and some are nearly always empty, and it is worth establishing which
is which before building anything on a field that turns out to be blank four
times in five.

```{r tbl-profile}
cols <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('%s')", c_url))

# Build one count(col) and one count(DISTINCT col) for every column, then run
# them all in a single pass rather than one query per column.
exprs <- sprintf(
  'count(%1$s) AS "%1$s__filled", count(DISTINCT %1$s) AS "%1$s__distinct"',
  cols$column_name)

raw <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT count(*) AS n_rows, %s FROM read_parquet('%s')",
  paste(exprs, collapse = ", "), c_url))

profile <- tibble::tibble(
  Column     = cols$column_name,
  Type       = cols$column_type,
  `% filled` = round(100 * as.numeric(raw[1, paste0(cols$column_name, "__filled")])
                     / raw$n_rows, 1),
  Distinct   = as.numeric(raw[1, paste0(cols$column_name, "__distinct")])
) |>
  arrange(`% filled`)

profile |>
  mutate(Distinct = format(Distinct, big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable(caption = "Every column in the contracts table, 2024 Q1, sorted by how often it is populated. The emptiest fields appear first.")
```

Table 3 splits into three groups. Twelve columns are present on every row, two
more are nearly complete, and everything else falls away steadily from
`term_name` at 74.7% down to `actual_termination_date` at 2.3% with no sharp
break anywhere, so each sparse field has to be judged on its own. The distinct
counts are informative too: `year_quarter` takes one value and carries nothing
within a quarter, while `contract_service_agreement_id` has 51,859 values
against 57,026 distinct contracts, confirming that sellers reuse IDs.

Two absences matter. Only 26.4% of rows record a delivery balancing authority
and 15.2% a receipt one, so most contracts do not say where the power went.
And while execution and commencement dates are on every row,
`contract_termination_date` is filled on 34.6%, which is why contract duration
is left out of this thesis and discussed in Section 9 instead.

Two patterns in that table are worth pulling out now, because they change how
the categorical fields should be read.

**Blank does not always mean missing.** `term_name` is empty in about a quarter
of rows and `class_name` in more than half, and since both are marked
unconditionally required in every version of FERC's data dictionary, the blanks
initially looked to me like a filing failure. They are not. FERC lists `N/A` as
an allowable *value* for both, defined as "to be used only when the other
available Class Names do not apply," and PUDL's transform converts the string
`N/A` to NULL [@pudlissues, issue #4850]. Filers appear to be correctly
reporting that firmness or term does not apply to a transmission or
interconnection agreement, and the cleaning step then erases the difference
between "not applicable" and "never reported."

The practical consequence is that `WHERE term_name IS NOT NULL` does not drop
bad records, it drops a category. **[CHECK]** Confirm against the raw FERC CSV
that the nulled rows do contain the literal string `N/A`.

**One categorical field is really two.** `product_type_name` looks like a
stable set of codes, but fifteen of its values are capacity reassignment
crossed with a time zone, so `CR-PP` is Pacific Prevailing, `CR-ED` is Eastern
Daylight, and so on. Those fifteen codes were introduced in version 3.5 of
FERC's data dictionary, effective 2021 Q1, and before that there was only plain
`CR` [@ferc2020dictionary]. Anyone grouping by this column across the full
decade will see capacity reassignment volume appear to collapse in 2021 and
fragment into sixteen pieces, with nothing having changed in the underlying
market.

## What is missing before you start

Three things are absent from the files, and a reader should know about all
three before trusting any total.

**Rows that never made it through.** PUDL drops records it cannot parse.
Roughly 0.6 percent of all EQR records, about 29 million rows, fail on CSV
quoting errors, and a further 922,000 fail on character encoding
[@pudlissues, issues #4928 and #4927]. Their pipeline diagnostics report
between 0.5 and 1.8 million records rejected per quarter [@pudlissues, issue
#5562]. 
None of this is flagged in the output. The rows are simply not there.

**Duplicates that have not been resolved.** The transactions table has no
enforced primary key, because duplicate rows persist across the history and the
cause has not been established. PUDL's own note says it "isn't yet clear
whether this reflects a data quality issue in the underlying FERC EQR
submissions or a bug in PUDL's extraction or transformation of this table"
[@pudlissues, issue #5455].

**The jurisdictional gaps** described above: ERCOT, Alaska, Hawaii, and small
non-public utilities.

None of these makes the data unusable. What they mean is that totals from this
dataset should be read as "what was filed and successfully parsed" rather than
as "what happened in the wholesale market," and those are different claims.
Section 5 takes up the variables that are present but do not mean what they
appear to mean, which is a larger problem than the one in this subsection.

# Getting the Data: Working with 80 GB from a Laptop

## Where the data lives

PUDL does not distribute the EQR as a single file, and it does not distribute
it as a database you log into either. It is a set of Apache Parquet files
sitting in public cloud storage, one file per table per quarter, at addresses
of the form

```
s3://pudl.catalyst.coop/ferceqr/<table>/<yyyyqQ>.parquet
```

Four tables across 52 quarters, 2013 Q3 through 2026 Q2, so a little over two
hundred files in total. The storage is public, so none of this requires an
account or credentials.

What that arrangement buys you is that the download step disappears. You write
a query naming the files you want, the query runs against the copies in cloud
storage, and a result comes back. For most of the work in this project I never
had the data on my own machine at all, which matters when the transactions
table runs to roughly 80 GB across its full history and my laptop has
considerably less free disk than that.

The engine doing the work is DuckDB, which runs inside the R session rather
than as a separate server you have to install and connect to. Its `httpfs`
extension lets it read files over the web, so `read_parquet()` takes a URL
where it would normally take a file path and nothing gets written to disk.
Everything from here on is ordinary SQL, sent from R with `dbGetQuery()` and
coming back as a data frame.

## Why the file format matters

A file is a one-dimensional sequence of bytes and a table is two-dimensional,
so any file format has to choose an order. A CSV writes one whole row, then the
next. Parquet writes one whole column, then the next, and records in a footer
where each column begins.

Two useful things follow from that choice. A query naming four of
thirty-two columns moves roughly four columns' worth of data rather than the
whole file, since the other twenty-eight are in stretches of the file that
never get read. And because identical values end up stored next to each other,
columns that repeat the same value over and over compress extremely well,
which is most of why a dataset this size is only 80 GB.

Combined with the quarterly split, that means the layout has already separated
the data along two axes. Narrowing by time opens fewer files, and narrowing by
column opens less of each file. Narrowing any other way means reading a column
to find out which rows you wanted, which the next subsection takes up.

One consequence is worth knowing immediately. Row counts come from the Parquet
footer rather than from the data, so counting rows does not read the data at
all, even on the transactions table.

```{r row-count}
# ASKS: how many rows in one quarter of transactions?
#   SELECT = what to return, count(*) = how many rows, AS = rename it
#   FROM read_parquet('...') = treat this file as a table
#   sprintf() drops the file address into the %s slot
n_tx <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT count(*) AS n_rows
     FROM read_parquet('%s')", t_url))$n_rows

format(n_tx, big.mark = ",")
```

One quarter of the transactions table holds
`r format(n_tx, big.mark = ",")` rows, and the query never touches the data to
work that out. Each Parquet file stores a summary of its own contents, so
DuckDB reads that summary instead of the rows. This is worth knowing early,
because it means you can always check how big something is before committing to
querying it.

## Anatomy of a query

Every query in this section is built out of the same handful of words, so it is
worth taking them one at a time, starting with the smallest query that does
anything useful.

```{r query-smallest}
# ASKS: what do a few rows actually look like?
#   SELECT = which columns to return
#   FROM read_parquet('...') = which file to treat as a table
#   LIMIT = stop after this many rows
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT seller_company_name, term_name, class_name
     FROM read_parquet('%s')
    LIMIT 5", c_url))
```

Three clauses, and the last one matters more than it looks, because without a
`LIMIT` that query would have tried to hand R every row in the file.

Now a real question. Contracts are labelled long-term or short-term, so how
many of each are there?

```{r query-grouped}
# ASKS: how many contracts of each term type?
#   WHERE = drop rows that fail a test
#   GROUP BY 1 = one output row per value of the first selected column
#   count(*) = how many rows landed in each group
#   ORDER BY = sort the result
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT term_name, count(*) AS n
     FROM read_parquet('%s')
    WHERE term_name IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY 1
    ORDER BY n DESC", c_url))
```

SQL is written in one order and executed in another, and reading it in
execution order is what made it click for me:

| Clause | What it does | Here |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM` | which file to treat as a table | one quarter of contracts |
| `WHERE` | drop rows that fail a test, one row at a time | drop rows with no term recorded |
| `GROUP BY` | collapse the surviving rows into groups | one group per term type |
| `SELECT` | what to return for each group | the term, and how many rows were in it |
| `ORDER BY` | sort the result | biggest group first |

Four conventions in there get reused by every query below. `count(*)` is an
**aggregate**, meaning it turns a whole group into one number, and `sum()`,
`avg()`, `min()` and `max()` work the same way; an aggregate needs a
`GROUP BY` to tell it what the groups are. `GROUP BY 1` means group by the
first thing in `SELECT`, and writing the column name again does exactly the
same thing. `AS` renames a column in the output, and without it the header is
the whole expression, which gets ugly fast. And `WHERE` filters rows before
grouping while `HAVING` filters groups after, which is the distinction I got
wrong most often when I was starting.

One caution on that `WHERE term_name IS NOT NULL` before moving on. It looks
like it is dropping bad records and it is not, it is dropping a category.
Section 5 explains why, and the short version is that FERC allows `N/A` as a
legitimate value and PUDL converts it to NULL during cleaning, so a blank term
usually means the concept does not apply rather than that nobody filled it in.

Everything else in this section is those two queries with more clauses added
on. The one habit worth forming now is naming your columns, because
`SELECT *` asks for all of them, which throws away the main advantage of the
format, and on the transactions table it is the difference between a query that
works and one that does not.

## Choosing what to read

A query can narrow what it reads in two different ways, and they work
differently. One is built into the storage layout. The other means reading a
column to find out which rows you wanted.

**Time is the partition.** Restricting to a period is not really a filter, it
is a choice of which files to open:

```{r subset-time}
# ASKS: how many rows in one quarter, then across all 52?
n_q  <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM read_parquet('%s')", c_url))$n   # quotes: one file
n_all <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM read_parquet(%s)", all_c))$n     # no quotes: a list

c(one_quarter = n_q, all_quarters = n_all)
```

One quarter of contracts holds `r format(n_q, big.mark = ",")` rows and all 52
quarters hold `r format(n_all, big.mark = ",")`. Restricting to a period never
reads a row and then discards it, because the rows that do not belong live in
files that were never opened.

Those two numbers are also worth setting against the transaction count above.
The entire contracts table, every quarter since 2013, is under ten million
rows, while a single quarter of transactions is over 140 million. When people
describe this dataset as large, the transactions table is what they mean, and
almost everything awkward about working with the EQR comes from that one table.

Two practical notes on the time axis. The data begins in 2013 Q3 and the most
recent quarter available usually lags the present by one quarter. Past filings
also get revised, sometimes years later, which Section 3 shows happening to
this project between October and November.

**Columns are the storage order**, for the reason given above, so naming four
of thirty-two moves roughly four columns' worth of data. This is the whole
reason to avoid `SELECT *`.

**Everything else is a filter**, which means reading a column to find the rows
that match. That still works, but it is a different kind of operation and
worth recognizing as one. The two filters you are most likely to want are
geography and contract type.

Geography is recorded as a balancing authority, and contracts carry one at each
end, the point of receipt and the point of delivery, while transactions carry
only delivery.

```{r subset-region}
# ASKS: which delivery regions appear most often in contracts?
# Same shape as the term query above, just a different column.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT point_of_delivery_balancing_authority AS ba, count(*) AS n
     FROM read_parquet('%s')
    WHERE point_of_delivery_balancing_authority IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY 1
    ORDER BY n DESC
    LIMIT 20", c_url))
```

**[TODO]** Describe the top regions once the terminology in Section 2 is
settled, since the codes do not mean much before then.

There is a large caveat on that query which took me a while to notice, and it
is the reason I would not build anything important on it. Only 26.4% of
contract rows record a delivery balancing authority at all, and 15.2% record a
receipt one, so the table above is describing roughly a quarter of the data
rather than all of it. The `WHERE ... IS NOT NULL` is doing far more work than
it appears to. Section 3 has the full fill rates. Where regional questions
matter in this thesis I use the transactions table instead, which is what
Section 6 does.

ERCOT barely appears here, and the reason is jurisdictional rather than
technical. Most wholesale sales inside ERCOT fall outside FERC's authority
because ERCOT is not synchronously interconnected with the rest of the
country, so they are never filed. A small number of contracts do record an
ERCOT delivery point, but against the size of the Texas market it is a
rounding error. Section 3 has the detail.

Contract type is spread across four categorical fields. Since the query is the
same each time and only the column name changes, it is worth wrapping in a
small R function rather than writing it out four times:

```{r subset-categoricals}
# ASKS: what values does a column take, and how often?
# Same query as above, with the column, file and row limit as arguments.
# %s takes text, %d takes a number.
val_counts <- function(col, url = c_url, n = 20) {
  dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
    "SELECT %s AS value, count(*) AS n
       FROM read_parquet('%s')
      GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT %d", col, url, n))
}

val_counts("term_name")          # LT (a year or more) vs ST
val_counts("class_name")         # firm, non-firm, unit power sale
val_counts("product_type_name")  # cost-based, market-based, transmission
val_counts("product_name")       # energy, capacity, ancillary services
```

Four queries in four lines, and the same function works on any column of any of
the four tables. Counting the values in a field is the standard first move on
an unfamiliar column, so this is worth keeping around.

The four fields are smaller than they look. `term_name` has only two values,
`class_name` three, `product_type_name` eleven and `product_name`
thirty-two, and the first two are blank on a quarter and a half of rows
respectively for the `N/A` reason above. **[TODO]** Describe what the main
values in each of the four actually mean, once Section 2 has introduced the
terminology.

One thing to know about all four is that they are not stable across the full
history. PUDL notes that FERC's published data dictionary has been revised
several times since 2013 and that the allowable values changed along the way,
and PUDL accepts any value that was valid in any version. Section 3 gives the
clearest example of what that does, where fifteen capacity-reassignment codes
appear in 2021 where there had previously been one.

## Querying the big table

Everything so far has used contracts, which is small enough that none of this
machinery would be necessary. Transactions is the table that makes this a
large-data problem, and the point of this subsection is that nothing about the
method changes.

The first move on an unfamiliar table is to see what is in it without reading
any of it. `DESCRIBE` returns the column names and types from the footer:

```{r describe-transactions}
# ASKS: what columns does the transactions table have, and of what type?
#   DESCRIBE reports the schema; it reads no rows at all.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('%s')", t_url))
```

Twenty-eight columns, and the ones that matter for most questions are
`seller_company_id_ferc`, `contract_service_agreement_id`, `product_name`,
`type_of_rate`, `point_of_delivery_balancing_authority`,
`standardized_price` and `standardized_quantity`. The first three are what
Section 6 uses to join transactions back to their contracts, and the last two
are the price and volume fields that Section 5 spends most of its time
warning about.

Now the same shape of query as before, on 143 million rows instead of 200
thousand:

```{r transactions-aggregate}
# ASKS: which delivery regions see the most transactions in one quarter?
# Same clauses as before. The only thing that changed is the file.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT point_of_delivery_balancing_authority AS ba, count(*) AS n
     FROM read_parquet('%s')
    WHERE point_of_delivery_balancing_authority IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY 1
    ORDER BY n DESC
    LIMIT 10", t_url))
```

That query is the whole argument for the format. It never asked for a row, only
for a count per group, so DuckDB read one column out of the file and nothing
else. Had this been a CSV it would have had to read all 143 million rows in
full to produce the same ten numbers.

The practical limit is on what you ask to come back, not on what you ask it to
look through. A query that groups 143 million rows into ten is fine. A query
that returns 143 million rows is not, and that distinction is what the next
subsection turns into a rule.

I should add one warning about the result, because it is a good example of a
query being correct and the answer being misleading. These are transaction
counts, and a transaction row in an organized market is a five-minute
settlement interval while a bilateral sale can be a whole month in one row. The
ranking above is therefore telling you which regions report most often, not
which regions trade most. Section 5 and Section 6 both take this up, and
Section 6 shows what the same question looks like when it is weighted by
energy.

## A worked example: filter, aggregate, pull down

To show the whole process on one question: how many contracts were active in
each quarter?

```{r worked-example}
# ASKS: for every quarter, how many distinct contracts were active?
#
# Counting rows would be wrong. A contract is re-reported every quarter it
# stays active and can take several rows within one quarter, so neither the
# row count nor either ID alone identifies a contract.
#   CAST(x AS VARCHAR) = treat x as text
#   concat_ws('|', a, b) = glue with a separator, skipping NULLs
# concat_ws rather than || is deliberate: || returns NULL if either side is
# NULL, and about 2% of rows have no seller ID, so || would silently drop
# them from the count. Section 5 measures what that costs.
counts <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT year_quarter,
         count(DISTINCT concat_ws('|',
                 CAST(seller_company_id_ferc AS VARCHAR),
                 contract_service_agreement_id)) AS n_contracts
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
   GROUP BY 1
   ORDER BY 1", all_c))

# "2024q1" -> 2024.00, so it plots on a sensible axis
counts <- counts |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(substr(year_quarter, 1, 4)) +
                (as.numeric(substr(year_quarter, 6, 6)) - 1) / 4)

# Pull out the values the text below refers to, so they cannot go stale.
pick     <- function(q) counts$n_contracts[counts$year_quarter == q]
open_q   <- pick("2013q3"); trough <- pick("2014q1")
y2018    <- pick("2018q1"); recent <- pick("2025q2")

ggplot(counts, aes(year, n_contracts)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2013.4, xmax = 2014.0,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "red", alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Contracts active",
       title = "Active electricity contracts by quarter, 2013 to 2026") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Three decisions in that query are worth naming.

The count is `count(DISTINCT ...)` on a composite key rather than `count(*)`,
for the reasons in Section 3. Contracts are restated in every quarter they stay
active and a single contract can occupy several rows within one quarter, so a
plain row count measures something other than contracts. The seller ID and the
service agreement ID together identify a contract and neither does it alone.

The aggregation happens remotely, and this is the pattern the rest of the
project depends on: filter and aggregate inside the query, then pull down only
the result. The query reads all 52 files and returns 52 rows, so what crosses
the network and lands in R's memory is small enough to plot no matter how large
the files behind it were. The alternative, pulling rows into R and summarizing
them there with `dplyr`, works fine on contracts and is not an option at all on
transactions.

And the result is not uniformly trustworthy, which is the part worth dwelling
on. The series opens at `r format(open_q, big.mark = ",")` contracts in 2013 Q3
and falls to `r format(trough, big.mark = ",")` by 2014 Q1, a drop of
`r round(100 * (open_q - trough) / open_q)`%. From
`r format(y2018, big.mark = ",")` in 2018 Q1 it rises to
`r format(recent, big.mark = ",")` by 2025 Q2, an increase of
`r round(100 * (recent - y2018) / y2018)`%. The two moves are similar in size,
and the second looks like a market trend while the first does not.

The reason to doubt the first is that 2013 Q3 is the opening quarter of FERC's
current reporting format. A way to check that is to ask what share of a
quarter's contracts have disappeared three quarters later, and compare the
opening quarter against ordinary ones.

```{r churn}
# ASKS: what share of one quarter's contracts are gone three quarters later?
# A contract still in force gets refiled, so disappearing means it ended.
keys <- function(q) dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT DISTINCT concat_ws('|', CAST(seller_company_id_ferc AS VARCHAR),
                  contract_service_agreement_id) AS k
    FROM read_parquet('%s')", eqr("core_ferceqr__contracts", q)))$k

churn <- function(q0, q3) round(100 * mean(!(keys(q0) %in% keys(q3))), 1)

data.frame(
  From = c("2013q3", "2015q1", "2019q1"),
  `Share gone three quarters later` =
    c(churn("2013q3", "2014q2"),
      churn("2015q1", "2015q4"),
      churn("2019q1", "2019q4")),
  check.names = FALSE)
```

Ordinary turnover sits around ten to twenty percent and the opening quarter
loses far more than that. That is consistent with the first filings containing
a one-time backlog of agreements that were then cleared off the books over the
following year, though I have not established the mechanism directly and would
not state it as more than a plausible reading.

The practical rule I would give is to treat the first two quarters of the data
as a separate regime rather than as the start of a series.

## Summary

The method, in four steps:

1. Name the files you want. Time is the partition.
2. Name the columns you want, and never `SELECT *`.
3. Filter and aggregate inside the query, where the data is.
4. Pull down only the result.

And what each dimension of the data looks like from a query:

| Dimension | How | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Time | Choose files; it is the partition | Starts 2013 Q3; runs a quarter behind; filings get revised |
| Columns | Name them in `SELECT` | Avoid `SELECT *` on transactions |
| Delivery region | `point_of_delivery_balancing_authority` | Recorded on only 26% of contract rows; strings, not a join key; essentially no ERCOT |
| Product, term, class | The four categorical fields | Blanks are a category, not missing data; allowable values changed over the decade |
| Seller and buyer | `seller_company_id_ferc`, `customer_company_name` | Sellers have an ID, buyers do not. See Sections 5 and 6 |
| State | Not available | `contact_state` is a mailing address, not geography. See Section 5 |
| Price | `rate` on contracts, `standardized_price` on transactions | Only half of contracts carry a rate, and the units live in a separate column. See Section 5 |
| Contract to transaction | Seller ID, agreement ID and product | Works, but see Section 6 for the caveats |


# What's Actually in There: Data Quality and Validation

Section 3 described what the EQR contains and Section 4 showed how to query it
without downloading any of it. This section is about the parts I got wrong on
the way there. Many findings below started the same way: I ran a query,
got back a number that looked reasonable, and only later found out
that it was not measuring what I thought it was measuring.

That pattern is worth taking seriously, because it is the reason a guide like
this one is useful at all. Many of the problems in this section did not announce
themselves. Often times no query failed, no column was obviously empty, and the
PUDL field catalog did not readily warn you of these. A user who reads the catalog,
writes a sensible aggregation, and reports the result will in several cases
publish a number that is wrong by a factor of two or more, and will have no way
of knowing. Documenting where those traps are is most of what I have to offer.

I have organized the findings by the kind of mistake each one causes rather
than going column by column, since the same underlying problem tends to turn up
in more than one place.

## A row is not a contract

The first thing I tried to do with this dataset was count contracts, which
turned out to be harder than it sounds. The contracts table for 2024 Q1 has
199,278 rows in it, and my initial assumption was that each row was an
agreement between a seller and a buyer. It is not, and there are two separate
reasons why.

The first is that a single agreement gets filed as one row per product and rate
combination, which I will call line splitting. The clearest example I found was
Allegheny Ridge Wind Farm's agreement with PJM, which appears as six separate
rows covering energy, capacity, spinning reserve, reactive supply and voltage
control, uplift, and a catch-all "other" category. All six share the same
agreement ID and nothing in any individual row marks it as part of something
larger, so if you are counting rows you have counted that one agreement six
times.

The second reason is restatement, which I think is the more dangerous of the
two because it only shows up once you start working across quarters. A
quarterly filing is not a list of contracts signed that quarter. Every seller
refiles every contract that is still in force, so a ten-year power purchase
agreement signed in 2016 shows up in all forty quarterly files that have been
published since. Stacking quarters and counting rows counts that contract once
per quarter.

FERC's intended identifier for a contract is the seller's company ID combined
with the agreement ID that the seller assigned to it, and neither piece is
unique on its own. Agreement IDs in particular are free text chosen by the
filer, and I found that the ID `1` is used by 66 different sellers and
`ISO-NE MPSA` by another 66, so the seller ID has to be part of the
key rather than being a nice-to-have.

```{r rows-vs-contracts}
# Three things at once: how many rows there are, how many actual contracts,
# and how much damage the obvious way of building the key does.
#   ||          glues text together, but returns NULL if either side is NULL
#   concat_ws   glues text together and skips NULLs instead
# The gap between the two key counts is contracts the first version loses.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT count(*) AS n_rows,
         count(DISTINCT CAST(seller_company_id_ferc AS VARCHAR) || '|' ||
                        contract_service_agreement_id)  AS keys_naive,
         count(DISTINCT concat_ws('|',
                        CAST(seller_company_id_ferc AS VARCHAR),
                        contract_service_agreement_id)) AS keys_safe,
         sum(CASE WHEN seller_company_id_ferc IS NULL
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                    AS rows_no_seller
    FROM read_parquet('%s')", c_url)) |>
  kable(caption = "Rows, contracts, and what NULL propagation costs.")
```

The table above gives three answers at once. The quarter has 199,278 rows but only
57,026 contracts, so the average agreement is split into about three and a half
rows and the row count overstates the number of agreements by a factor of three.

The other two columns are there because of a mistake I made early on. 4,120
rows, just over 2% of the table, have no seller company ID recorded. When I
first built the composite key I used SQL's `||` operator to glue the two pieces
together, which is the obvious way to do it, and I did not realize that `||`
returns NULL if either input is NULL. Every one of those 4,120 rows produced a
NULL key, and `count(DISTINCT)` throws NULLs away without any warning, so the
query ran cleanly and returned 56,205 instead of 57,026. That is 821 contracts
quietly missing, a difference of about one and a half percent, which is small
enough that I never would have caught it by looking at the answer. `concat_ws`
skips the NULL rather than propagating it, which is why I use it everywhere in
this guide. I think this is the easiest mistake to make with the EQR and the
single hardest one to notice, because both versions return a number that looks
perfectly sensible.

The restatement problem is much larger, and it only appears once you stack
quarters.

```{r restatement}
# One row per contract per quarter, then stack. If each quarter's file held
# only new contracts, three quarters would give roughly three times as many
# distinct contracts as one quarter does. It does not.
qs <- c("2023q3", "2023q4", "2024q1")

stacked <- lapply(qs, function(q) {
  dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
    SELECT DISTINCT '%s' AS yq,
           concat_ws('|', CAST(seller_company_id_ferc AS VARCHAR),
                          contract_service_agreement_id) AS contract_key
      FROM read_parquet('%s')", q, eqr("core_ferceqr__contracts", q)))
}) |> bind_rows()

tibble(
  quarters           = length(qs),
  contract_rows      = nrow(stacked),
  distinct_contracts = n_distinct(stacked$contract_key),
  pct_duplicated     = round(100 * (1 - n_distinct(stacked$contract_key) /
                                        nrow(stacked)), 1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Stacking three quarters of contracts without de-duplicating.")

# How many of the three quarters does a given contract turn up in?
stacked |>
  count(contract_key, name = "n_quarters") |>
  count(n_quarters, name = "n_contracts") |>
  kable(caption = "Quarters each contract appears in.")
```

Three quarters of data produce 170,869 contract-quarter pairs but only 65,021
distinct contracts, so 61.9% of what you would get by stacking the files is
duplication. The second table shows why that number is so high: 51,282 of the 65,021
contracts, which is 78.9% of them, appear in all three quarters. Only 10,455
appear in exactly one. The EQR is much closer to a snapshot of everything
currently in force than it is to a log of new activity, and I had the mental
model backwards for the first several weeks of working with it.

The practical consequence is that any analysis spanning more than one quarter
needs an explicit de-duplication step, and that step is not optional or
cosmetic. What I settled on is to take `DISTINCT` on the composite key within
each quarter first, stack the quarters, and then take `DISTINCT` again across
them, keeping the most recent filing in cases where I need the contract's
terms rather than just its existence. A small share of keys, something like
half a percent, come back with more than one contract execution date attached,
which means the seller reused an agreement ID for a genuinely different deal.
There is no automatic way to resolve those, so I either handle them by hand or
drop them and say so.

## Half of the contracts have no price

The most obvious reason to use the EQR instead of some other dataset is that it
reports prices, which almost nothing else at this level of detail does. It
reports them for about half of the rows.

```{r rate-fill}
# How much of the contracts table carries a usable price at all. count(col)
# only counts non-NULL values, so comparing it to count(*) gives a fill rate.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT count(*)          AS n_rows,
         count(rate)       AS has_rate,
         count(rate_units) AS has_units,
         round(100.0 * count(rate) / count(*), 1) AS pct_with_rate
    FROM read_parquet('%s')", c_url)) |>
  kable(caption = "How many contract rows carry a price?")
```

105,463 of the 199,278 rows have a rate recorded, which works out to 52.9%. I
was initially worried this was a reporting failure, but after looking at which
rows are missing a price it mostly is not. The rows without one are
overwhelmingly agreements that do not have a price in the ordinary sense:
membership agreements, interconnection agreements, and network and
point-to-point transmission service. A membership agreement in an RTO does not
have a dollars-per-megawatt-hour figure attached to it, so there is nothing for
the seller to report.

That said, it still matters for anyone doing price work, because it means you
are working with half the table and the half you keep is not a random sample of
it. Any claim about "average contract prices in the EQR" is really a claim
about the subset of agreements that are priced sales, and that subset skews
toward energy and capacity products and away from transmission.

The smaller number in that table bothered me more. 105,463 rows have a rate but
only 101,292 have a rate unit, which leaves 4,171 rows reporting a price with
no denominator attached. A rate of 45 with no unit could be $45 per megawatt
hour or $45 per kilowatt-month, and those differ by roughly three orders of
magnitude, so there seems to be no way to recover what was meant.

## The number and its units are stored separately

This brings me to the next field that brought me trouble. `rate` holds the
price and `rate_units` holds what the price is per, and they are stored in
separate columns with no validation linking them.

```{r rate-units}
# Printing the data frame gives plain verbatim output rather than a formatted
# table. I do it that way here because several of the unit codes start with a
# slash, and the table renderer mangles them badly enough to be unreadable.
ru <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT rate_units, count(*) AS n
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC", c_url))

nrow(ru)
print(head(ru, 15))
```

There are 21 distinct unit codes and the top fifteen cover 99.8% of rows, so
the vocabulary itself is clean and well controlled, which was a pleasant
surprise after everything else in this section. `$/MWH` accounts for 77,830
rows and `FLAT RATE` for 9,848, and after that there is a long tail of
capacity-style units including `$/KW-MO`, `$/MW-MO`, `$/KW-YR`, `$/MW-DAY` and
so on, plus 97 rows still reported in `CENTS/KWH`.

The consequence is that `avg(rate)` means nothing at all unless you have
already filtered to one unit, and this is the trap I actually fell into. When I
first compared contracted prices against realized transaction prices for
Section 6, I averaged `rate` across every row that had one, which mixed
dollars-per-megawatt-hour energy prices together with dollars-per-kilowatt-month
capacity charges. Because both are small positive numbers the output looked
entirely plausible, and it took me a while to work out why some of the ratios
were coming back in the thousands. Every price query in this guide filters on
`rate_units` before it does anything else, and I would recommend that anyone
else do the same.

## A fifth of transaction quantities are negative

The transactions table is where the actual volume lives, and
`standardized_quantity` is the natural column to sum if you want to know how
much energy changed hands. Summing it directly gives the wrong answer, and I
only discovered this because a percentage came back negative.

```{r negative-quantity}
# Roughly 20% of rows have a negative quantity. Breaking that down by rate type
# shows whether it is a defect spread across the table or a real category.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT type_of_rate,
         count(*) AS n,
         round(100.0 * sum(CASE WHEN standardized_quantity < 0
                           THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / count(*), 1) AS pct_negative
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE standardized_quantity IS NOT NULL
   GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 10", t_url)) |>
  kable(caption = "Where negative quantities come from.")
```

29,309,795 of the 143,442,727 transaction rows carry a negative quantity, which
is 20.4% of the table. My first thought was that this had to be a data entry
problem, but the table above makes it fairly clear that it is structural instead. Rows
priced through an RTO or ISO are negative 22.3% of the time and index-priced
rows 14.1% of the time, while rows with a fixed negotiated price are negative
0.0% of the time. Negative quantities belong to market settlement reporting and
essentially never appear in bilateral deals, which is too clean a split to be
random error.

What they actually represent is most likely the buy side of a settlement, where
a participant is taking power out of the market rather than delivering it into
it, but I want to be careful here because neither the PUDL field catalog nor
FERC's data dictionary says so explicitly. **[TODO]** Confirm this against the
FERC filing instructions before I state it as fact in the final draft.

Regardless of the underlying reason, the practical consequence is not
ambiguous. `sum(standardized_quantity)` returns a net position rather than a
volume. In the regional analysis in Section 6 this produced an organized-market
share of negative 11.2% for one balancing authority, which was obvious enough
to catch. What worries me more is that in a region where the buy and sell sides
happen to be less balanced, the same error would have returned something like
45% and I would have written it up without a second thought.

## Prices and quantities have impossible tails

```{r price-tails}
# What is actually in the price and quantity columns. approx_quantile is a
# sampling-based percentile rather than an exact one, which is why it runs
# cheaply on 143 million rows, and also why it moves slightly between runs.
dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT round(min(standardized_price), 2)                   AS p_min,
         round(approx_quantile(standardized_price, 0.50), 2) AS p_median,
         round(approx_quantile(standardized_price, 0.99), 2) AS p99,
         round(max(standardized_price), 2)                   AS p_max,
         round(approx_quantile(standardized_quantity, 0.50), 2) AS q_median,
         round(max(standardized_quantity), 2)                AS q_max,
         sum(CASE WHEN standardized_price < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS neg_price
    FROM read_parquet('%s')", t_url)) |>
  kable(caption = "Distribution of transaction price and quantity.")
```

The middle of the distribution looks fine. The median transaction price is
$22.51 per megawatt hour and the 99th percentile is $188.04, both of which are
ordinary wholesale prices and both of which gave me some confidence that the
column means what it says it means.

The tails are another matter. The minimum price in the quarter is -$9,345,732
and the maximum is $44,675,000, and the largest single transaction quantity is
20,865,178 MWh, which is more energy than most US states consume in a month.
Negative prices are a real phenomenon in wholesale markets, since generators
will sometimes pay to keep running when output is high and demand is low, so
the 8,213,514 rows with a negative price are not by themselves suspicious. A
price of negative nine million dollars per megawatt hour is a filing error. Any
analysis of prices in this dataset has to trim the tails, and whatever
threshold gets used needs to be reported alongside the result, because the
extremes are large enough to move a mean by several orders of magnitude on
their own.

The median quantity is the other number I would pull out of that table. At 0.04
MWh, the typical row in this table represents something like three minutes of a
small generator's output. That single figure says more about what the
transactions table actually is than anything in the documentation does, because
it makes clear that a row here is not a deal in any meaningful sense. It is one
settlement interval.

## Counting rows does not measure activity

This last one is really the trap that all the others are special cases of, and
it follows directly from the median quantity above.

A row in the transactions table is one reporting interval, and how long that
interval is depends entirely on how the seller participates in the market. An
RTO settlement gets reported every five minutes, so one seller operating under
one market agreement can generate tens of thousands of rows in a single
quarter. A monthly bilateral block sold at a fixed price is one row. To
`count(*)` these are both worth exactly one.

The size of the distortion surprised me. Rows priced through an RTO or ISO make
up 128.4 million of the 132.3 million transaction rows that have a reported
quantity, which is 97% of the table. Taken at face value that would mean the
United States has essentially no bilateral wholesale market, which is plainly
false, and which contradicts the market structure I described in Section 2.
What it actually measures is that organized markets report much more often.
Section 6 runs the same regional question weighted by energy instead of rows
and gets a very different picture.

The general rule I would give anyone picking this dataset up is that `count(*)`
on the transactions table answers a question about filing behavior and almost
never answers the question you meant to ask. Anything that is supposed to be
about market activity has to be weighted by quantity, and anything weighted by
