quantity has to deal with the negative values from the previous subsection
first.

## What to trust

Pulling all of this together, The table below is the summary I wish I had been handed
at the start of this project.

| Variable | Status | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `seller_company_id_ferc` | Reliable | Missing on 2% of contract rows; use `concat_ws` |
| `contract_service_agreement_id` | Reliable | Not unique without the seller ID |
| `product_name` | Reliable | Needed as part of the contract key |
| `rate` | Usable | Only alongside `rate_units`; absent on 47% of rows |
| `rate_units` | Reliable | Clean 21-value vocabulary |
| `standardized_price` | Usable | Trim the tails and report the threshold |
| `standardized_quantity` | Usable | Handle the 20% negative rows explicitly |
| `point_of_delivery_balancing_authority` | Usable | Frequently NULL |
| `contact_state` | Misleading | A mailing address, not an operating location |
| `term_name` on transactions | Unreliable | Long-term rows that are five-minute blocks |
| `class_name` | Partial | Blank on most non-transmission products |
| Row counts | Misleading | Measure reporting granularity, not activity |

**[TODO]** Fold in the three remaining items I have results for but have not
written up yet: the buyer name inconsistency test, the `contact_state`
demonstration showing it is a mailing address, and the 2013 Q3 reporting
discontinuity.

# Worked Examples: Questions This Data Can Answer

The previous two sections were about getting at the data and about what breaks
once you have it. This section is the payoff, where I take three questions that
someone would actually want to ask and work each one through end to end. All
three run on 2024 Q1 unless I say otherwise, and all three are deliberately
scoped so that I can defend every number in them rather than reaching for
something more ambitious that I would have to hedge.

The three questions are whether the market structure I described in Section 2
can be recovered from the data itself, whether a transaction can be traced back
to the contract it was sold under, and whether EQR sellers can be matched to
their identities in EIA's datasets. The first is a check on the data against
something already known. The second and third are both attempts at things that,
as far as I can tell, have not been published anywhere, and in both cases the
limits of what works turn out to be as informative as the result.

## Recovering market structure from the data

Section 2 described a wholesale market split between organized RTO and ISO
markets, which cover roughly two thirds of US load, and bilateral trade, which
dominates in the Southeast and much of the West. The transactions table should
be able to show that directly, because `type_of_rate` records whether a sale
was priced through an organized market or negotiated some other way, and
`point_of_delivery_balancing_authority` records where the power was delivered.

My first attempt at this counted transactions, and it failed in a way that is
worth reporting because it is such a clean illustration of the problem from
Section 5. Counting rows, every major region came back somewhere between 85%
and 100% organized, including PacifiCorp East and Bonneville, which are not in
an RTO at all. The query was correct and the answer was nonsense, because an
RTO settlement is reported every five minutes while a bilateral block is
reported once a month, so the row count was measuring how often each region
files rather than what it trades.

Weighting by energy instead fixes it.

```{r region-volume}
# For each delivery region: what share of its activity went through an
# organized market, measured two different ways?
# Positive and negative quantity are kept apart, because a fifth of rows are
# negative (Section 5) and summing them raw gives a net position, not a volume.
region_vol <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT point_of_delivery_balancing_authority AS ba,
         sum(CASE WHEN standardized_quantity > 0
                  THEN standardized_quantity ELSE 0 END)           AS pos_mwh,
         sum(CASE WHEN standardized_quantity < 0
                  THEN -standardized_quantity ELSE 0 END)          AS neg_mwh,
         sum(CASE WHEN type_of_rate = 'RTO/ISO'
                   AND standardized_quantity > 0
                  THEN standardized_quantity ELSE 0 END)           AS rto_pos_mwh,
         count(*)                                                  AS n_rows,
         sum(CASE WHEN type_of_rate = 'RTO/ISO' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rto_rows
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE point_of_delivery_balancing_authority IS NOT NULL
     AND standardized_quantity IS NOT NULL
   GROUP BY 1
  HAVING sum(CASE WHEN standardized_quantity > 0
                  THEN standardized_quantity ELSE 0 END) > 0
   ORDER BY pos_mwh DESC", t_url))

# Both weightings side by side, since the gap between them is the whole point.
region_vol |>
  mutate(pct_rto_rows = round(100 * rto_rows / n_rows, 1),
         pct_rto_mwh  = round(100 * rto_pos_mwh / pos_mwh, 1)) |>
  select(ba, n_rows, pct_rto_rows, pos_mwh, pct_rto_mwh) |>
  head(20) |>
  kable(caption = "Organized market share by delivery region, weighted by transaction count and by delivered energy, 2024 Q1.")
```

The table above puts the two measures next to each other and they disagree almost
everywhere. PacifiCorp East is the starkest case: 97.6% of its transactions are
priced through an organized market but only 3.7% of its energy is. WACM goes
from 77.8% to 10.0% and the Public Service Company of Colorado footprint from
84.3% to 7.8%. Reading down the energy column instead of the row column, the
regions separate into three groups that match what Section 2 described.

The first group is the genuine RTOs, where both measures are high and the
energy share lands somewhere between 75% and 85%. PJM comes in at 79.3%, MISO
at 75.1%, ISO New England at 75.2% and NYISO at 84.6%. Even here the energy
share is well below the transaction share, which I read as bilateral deals
inside an RTO footprint being individually much larger than five-minute market
settlements, so they get heavily underweighted by any row count.

The second group is the West, where the balancing authority sits inside a
real-time imbalance market but most energy still moves bilaterally. PacifiCorp
East at 3.7%, WACM at 10.0% and PSCO at 7.8% all fall here. This is consistent
with how the Western Energy Imbalance Market works, since it only clears
real-time imbalances rather than serving as a full day-ahead energy market, so
the organized share of transactions is high while the organized share of energy
stays small. CAISO at 30.8% sits awkwardly between the first two groups, and I
would want to look harder at how much of the energy delivered into CISO is
imported under bilateral arrangements before saying anything confident about it.

The third group is the Southeast, which has essentially no organized market at
all and shows it on both measures. Southern Company comes back at 0.1% by
energy, Duke at 0.0%, South Carolina at 0.0% and Carolina Power & Light East at
0.0%.

```{r region-plot}
#| fig-cap: "Share of activity priced through an organized market in each delivery region, measured by transaction count and by delivered energy, 2024 Q1. The dashed line is where the two measures would agree. Every region falls below it. The four Southeastern authorities (SOCO, DUK, SC, CPLE) sit on top of one another at the origin."

# Every region would fall on the diagonal if the two measures agreed.
# Labels sit to the left of the points because most regions cluster against
# the right edge, where labels placed above collide and get dropped.
region_vol |>
  slice_max(pos_mwh, n = 25) |>
  mutate(pct_rto_rows = 100 * rto_rows / n_rows,
         pct_rto_mwh  = 100 * rto_pos_mwh / pos_mwh) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct_rto_rows, pct_rto_mwh)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ba), size = 2.6, hjust = 1.2, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-20, 105), ylim = c(-2, 105)) +
  labs(x = "Percent of transactions priced through an RTO/ISO",
       y = "Percent of energy priced through an RTO/ISO") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

Figure 1 shows the same comparison as a scatter, one point per region, with the
row-count measure on the horizontal axis and the energy measure on the vertical.
The dashed line is where the two would agree. Every region falls below it, and
the vertical drop is the size of the overstatement.

What this example does not show is anything about load or market size. Power
gets resold as it moves between parties, so the same megawatt hour can appear
several times and PJM's 385 million MWh is well above what PJM actually
consumed. The shares hold up as shares; the totals are not energy consumed.

## Tracing a transaction back to its contract

The EQR publishes contracts and transactions as separate tables, and the
obvious question is whether a given sale can be connected to the agreement it
happened under. If it can, then the transactions table stops being an
anonymous stream of prices and quantities and becomes something you can attach
contract terms to. Before running this I expected the answer to be no, partly
because nothing I read suggested anyone had done it and partly because the
earlier draft of this thesis asserted it was unresolved.

FERC's data dictionary says that the transaction record carries a contract
service agreement ID, which is supposed to point back at the contract, so there
was at least a candidate key. The first thing I checked was whether it is
actually filled in, and it is, on all 143,442,727 transaction rows in the
quarter. The seller ID is slightly less complete, missing on 191,363 rows, or
0.13%.

Joining on seller ID and agreement ID alone worked, in the sense that all
10,308 distinct key combinations in the transactions table matched a contract.
But only 57% of those keys pointed at exactly one contract row, and the rest
pointed at as many as nine, which would multiply the data on any real join. The
reason turned out to be the line splitting from Section 5. Allegheny Ridge Wind
Farm's agreement with PJM is one agreement ID split across six contract rows by
product, and since transactions also record a product, adding `product_name` to
the key should resolve most of it.

```{r join-test}
# Collapse each table to one row per candidate key: seller, agreement and
# product. The transactions side is the expensive step, a single pass over
# three columns of a very large table. Everything after works on the result.
tx2 <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT seller_company_id_ferc, contract_service_agreement_id, product_name,
         count(*) AS n_transactions
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE contract_service_agreement_id IS NOT NULL
   GROUP BY 1, 2, 3", t_url))

# Carry a count of priced rows through, so the join can be scored on whether
# the contract it lands on actually has a rate attached.
ct2 <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT seller_company_id_ferc, contract_service_agreement_id, product_name,
         count(*)    AS n_contract_rows,
         count(rate) AS n_with_rate
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE contract_service_agreement_id IS NOT NULL
   GROUP BY 1, 2, 3", c_url))

key3 <- c("seller_company_id_ferc", "contract_service_agreement_id",
          "product_name")

# Cast the IDs to text on both sides so the join cannot fail on a type mismatch.
fix   <- function(d) d |> mutate(across(all_of(key3[1:2]), as.character))
both2 <- inner_join(fix(tx2), fix(ct2), by = key3)

tibble(
  tx_keys          = nrow(tx2),
  joined_keys      = nrow(both2),
  pct_tx_joined    = round(100 * sum(both2$n_transactions) /
                                 sum(tx2$n_transactions), 1),
  pct_one_to_one   = round(100 * mean(both2$n_contract_rows == 1), 1),
  pct_tx_with_rate = round(100 *
    sum(both2$n_transactions[both2$n_with_rate > 0]) /
    sum(tx2$n_transactions), 1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Joining transactions to contracts on seller, agreement ID and product.")
```

That table says the join works. 14,360 of the 14,895 key combinations match, and
because the ones that fail are small, 99.9% of all 143 million transaction rows
land on a contract filed in the same quarter. Adding the product to the key also
pushed one-to-one matching from 57% up to 82.7%, which confirms that the
fan-out was line splitting and not a defect in the key.

A mechanical match is not the same as a correct one though, and with numbers
this clean I wanted an independent check that the contracts being picked out are
really the contracts those sales happened under. The way to test that is price.
If the join is finding the right agreement, then the price written into the
contract should roughly match the prices actually realized on the transactions
underneath it, and there is no reason a coincidental match would produce that.

```{r price-validation}
# Only contracts I can compare cleanly: energy sales, priced in one unit, with
# a non-zero rate. Averaging across rate_units would be meaningless (Section 5).
ct_price <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT seller_company_id_ferc, contract_service_agreement_id, product_name,
         round(avg(rate), 2) AS contract_rate
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE rate > 0 AND rate_units = '$/MWH' AND product_name = 'ENERGY'
   GROUP BY 1, 2, 3", c_url))

nrow(ct_price)   # how many keys the comparison can use at all

# Hand that small table to DuckDB so the join runs inside the database rather
# than pulling 143 million rows into R.
duckdb_register(con, "ck", ct_price)

tx_price <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT t.seller_company_id_ferc,
         t.contract_service_agreement_id,
         t.product_name,
         count(*)                               AS n_tx,
         round(median(t.standardized_price), 2) AS realized_med
    FROM read_parquet('%s') t
    JOIN ck k
      ON t.seller_company_id_ferc        = k.seller_company_id_ferc
     AND t.contract_service_agreement_id = k.contract_service_agreement_id
     AND t.product_name                  = k.product_name
   -- Trim the tails established in Section 5, and keep deliveries only.
   WHERE t.standardized_price BETWEEN 0 AND 1000
     AND t.standardized_quantity > 0
   GROUP BY 1, 2, 3", t_url))

compare <- inner_join(tx_price, ct_price, by = key3) |>
  filter(realized_med > 0) |>
  mutate(ratio = realized_med / contract_rate)

tibble(
  n_keys        = nrow(compare),
  med_contract  = round(median(compare$contract_rate), 2),
  med_realized  = round(median(compare$realized_med), 2),
  med_ratio     = round(median(compare$ratio), 2),
  pct_within_25 = round(100 * mean(compare$ratio > 0.75 &
                                   compare$ratio < 1.25), 1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Contracted price against realized transaction price for the same key.")
```

3,393 contract keys meet the conditions and 3,048 of them have matching
transactions. Across those, the median contracted price is $34.60 per megawatt
hour and the median realized price is $34.34, giving a median ratio of exactly
1, and 94.9% of keys land within 25% of their contracted price. I did not
expect agreement that close. A mechanical key match could happen by accident,
but three thousand independent agreements each producing a realized price
within a few percent of what the contract says is not something coincidence
produces, so I am treating this as confirmation that the join is
right and not just structurally valid.

The honest limits are worth stating clearly. Only 23.2% of transaction volume
lands on a contract that carries a price at all, since most of the volume sits
under RTO market participation agreements where the contract has no rate and
there is nothing to compare. The price validation therefore runs on a slice of
the data rather than all of it. And everything here is one quarter. The
corresponding check on 2018 Q3 is written but has not been run yet, and until
it has I would describe this as a result for 2024 Q1 rather than a property of
the dataset. **[TO RUN]** The earlier-quarter check.

## Matching EQR sellers to EIA utilities

The EQR identifies a seller by a FERC company ID and a free-text name and
nothing else. There is no plant identifier, no location, and no link to any
other federal dataset, so you can see that a company sold power without knowing
what it owns or where it operates. My advisor suggested trying to close that
gap by matching seller names against EIA's utility records, which would give
access to capacity, technology and plant coordinates.

The approach is a normalization ladder: apply progressively more aggressive
cleaning to both sides and see how the match rate responds. The important rule
is that both name lists go through the identical function, since a match only
means something if the two names were transformed the same way.

```{r crosswalk}
# EQR sellers for the quarter, with a row count so matches can be weighted by
# how much of the data each seller accounts for.
eqr_sellers <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT seller_company_id_ferc, seller_company_name, count(*) AS n_rows
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE seller_company_name IS NOT NULL
   GROUP BY 1, 2", c_url))

# Every utility EIA knows about. This table is not partitioned by quarter.
eia_utils <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT DISTINCT utility_id_eia, utility_name_eia
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE utility_name_eia IS NOT NULL", pudl("core_eia__entity_utilities")))

# Four levels, each more aggressive than the last.
norm1 <- function(x) str_squish(str_to_upper(x))                 # case, spaces
norm2 <- function(x) str_squish(str_replace_all(norm1(x),         # punctuation
                                                "[^A-Z0-9 ]", " "))
SUFFIX <- "\\b(LLC|L L C|LP|LLP|INC|INCORPORATED|CO|CORP|CORPORATION|COMPANY|LTD|LIMITED|PLC|HOLDINGS?)\\b"
norm3 <- function(x) str_squish(str_remove_all(norm2(x), SUFFIX)) # corp suffix
FILLER <- "\\b(THE|OF|AND|ELECTRIC|POWER|ENERGY|UTILITIES|UTILITY|SERVICES?|GENERATION|MARKETING|RESOURCES)\\b"
norm4 <- function(x) str_squish(str_remove_all(norm3(x), FILLER)) # filler words

for (nm in c("L1", "L2", "L3", "L4")) {
  f <- get(paste0("norm", substr(nm, 2, 2)))
  eqr_sellers[[nm]] <- f(eqr_sellers$seller_company_name)
  eia_utils[[nm]]   <- f(eia_utils$utility_name_eia)
}

# Two rates per level, because they answer different questions. pct_sellers is
# about companies; pct_rows is about how much of the table gets covered.
match_at <- function(level) {
  hit <- eqr_sellers[[level]] %in% eia_utils[[level]]
  tibble(level       = level,
         n_matched   = sum(hit),
         pct_sellers = round(100 * mean(hit), 1),
         pct_rows    = round(100 * sum(eqr_sellers$n_rows[hit]) /
                                   sum(eqr_sellers$n_rows), 1))
}

bind_rows(lapply(c("L1", "L2", "L3", "L4"), match_at)) |>
  kable(caption = "Match rate between 2,760 EQR seller names and 17,498 EIA utility names at four levels of normalization.")
```

The table above shows the ladder flattening out. Matching on case and whitespace alone
gets 30.9% of sellers, stripping punctuation gets 43.6%, and stripping
corporate suffixes gets 50.7%, which is the single largest jump and reflects
how often the same company is "Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC" in one dataset and
"Duke Energy Carolinas LLC" in the other. The fourth level, which removes
filler words like ENERGY and POWER, buys only another 2.6 percentage points
and starts doing real damage: at that level eleven distinct EIA utilities
collapse onto INTERNATIONAL PAPER and ten onto CALPINE, so any match made there
is a coin flip. I stop at level three for everything that follows.

A 50.7% match rate initially looked like a failure of the method, but sorting
the unmatched sellers by size suggested otherwise. The largest misses are Tri-
State Generation and Transmission, Bonneville Power Administration, MISO,
CAISO, SPP, and a long list of pure trading companies like NextEra Energy
Marketing and Shell Energy North America. None of those are name problems.
Market operators, federal power marketing agencies and traders do not own
generators, so they are not in EIA-860 and never could be. That suggested the
match rate is really a property of what kind of company is filing, which is
testable.

```{r crosswalk-strata}
# Classify each seller by what they actually sold. A unit power sale is power
# from specific named generating units, which is strong evidence of ownership.
seller_type <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT seller_company_id_ferc, seller_company_name,
         max(CASE WHEN class_name = 'UP' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unit_power,
         max(CASE WHEN product_name IN ('ENERGY','CAPACITY')
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                        AS energy_cap,
         max(CASE WHEN product_name IN
             ('POINT-TO-POINT AGREEMENT','NETWORK','INTERCONNECTION AGREEMENT',
              'TRANSMISSION OWNERS AGREEMENT','NETWORK OPERATING AGREEMENT')
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                        AS transmission
    FROM read_parquet('%s')
   WHERE seller_company_name IS NOT NULL
   GROUP BY 1, 2", c_url))

seller_type <- seller_type |>
  mutate(
    # RTOs and ISOs are market operators, not utilities. They will never be in
    # EIA-860, so they should be identified rather than counted as misses.
    is_rto = str_detect(seller_company_name,
      regex(paste("independent system operator", "interconnection, l",
                  "power pool", "ISO New England", "Midcontinent",
                  sep = "|"), ignore_case = TRUE)),
    category = case_when(
      is_rto            ~ "RTO / ISO",
      unit_power   == 1 ~ "Sells unit power (owns plants)",
      energy_cap   == 1 ~ "Sells energy or capacity",
      transmission == 1 ~ "Transmission only",
      TRUE              ~ "Other"),
    L3 = norm3(seller_company_name))

seller_type |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(n_sellers = n(),
            matched   = sum(L3 %in% eia_utils$L3),
            pct       = round(100 * mean(L3 %in% eia_utils$L3), 1),
            .groups   = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(n_sellers)) |>
  kable(caption = "Match rate against EIA utilities, by what the seller actually sells.")
```

That last table is the result I would keep if I could only keep one from this example.
Sellers that make unit power sales, meaning power from specific named
generating units, match 58.1% of the time. Sellers of generic energy or
capacity match 47.3%. Transmission-only sellers match 11.1% and RTOs match
5.6%. The match rate is not really telling you how good the string matching
is, it is telling you whether the company owns generators, which is exactly
what determines whether EIA has heard of it.

One caveat on how the table is built. The RTO group is identified by pattern
matching on company names rather than by anything recorded in the data, and
the line between "transmission only" and "other" depends on which product
names I chose to list, so both are judgment calls I made rather than
categories the EQR provides. The headline result is not sensitive to that,
since unit power sellers match roughly ten times as often as RTOs either way,
but the individual percentages would shift a little under a different set of
rules.

Two further checks are worth mentioning briefly. Of the sellers that do match,
93.6% map to exactly one EIA utility rather than several, so the matches are
mostly unambiguous. And for those where a plant fleet could be pulled from
EIA's generator table, the balancing authority of the plants agreed with the
balancing authority the contracts deliver into for 87.9% of unit power
sellers, which is an independent check that does not use names at all.


# An Interactive Tool

**[Not yet drafted. Scope still to be discussed.]**

*A potential dashboard for exploring contract trends by region, date range and contract
type without writing code, built for policymakers, industry analysts and the
public.*

# Ethical Considerations

Most of this project is methodological, but making a dataset easier to use is not always necessarily an ethically neutral act. Three main issues came up, and I will go over how I delt with each.

## Personal information in the filer identity table

One of the four EQR tables, `quarterly_identity`, is a directory of the people who submit filings. It contains named individuals with their work email addresses, phone numbers, and street addresses. There are hundreds of thousands of these records across the full history.

This information is lawfully public and required by the FERC. That does not mean it is appropriate for me to reproduce it. The people listed are mostly mid-level compliance staff who provided a contact for a regulatory filing, not public figures who consented to scrutinty. 

I handled this by using the identity table only at the company level. Every query I ran against it returns company identifiers and company names, and none of the output in this document includes a contact name, email, phone number or street address. The one place I used a contact-level field was `contact_state`, and I used it only in aggregate, to show that it is a mailing address rather than geography. I also do not redistribute any of the data. A reader who wants it goes to PUDL, which is where I got it.

## Commercially sensitive pricing

The transactions table records what specific companies charged specific buyers for specific products. That is competitively sensitive information by any ordinary standard, and the point of this project is to make it easier to analyze.

The standard worry about price transparency in concentrated markets is that it can facilitate tacit coordination. If sellers can observe what rivals charged and to whom, they can stop undercutting each other without ever communicating. Buyers pay more, and so do the retail customers downstream. This is not hypothetical in wholesale electricity, where the California crisis of 2000 and 2001 was driven partly by "a combination of real scarcity and generator market power" [@borenstein2015restructuring, p. 8].

What makes me comfortable proceeding is that this decision was made deliberately, and not by me.

FERC considered exactly how much detail to require and rejected aggregation on statutory grounds. In Order No. 2001-A the Commission concluded that "aggregated data do not provide sufficient disclosure of rates to the public" and that "section 205(c) does not allow the aggregation of this information" [@ferc2023filing, p. 26]. The operational rule follows from that: "Transaction data may not be aggregated. If the price changes even on a sub-hourly basis, a new line of transaction data must be reported for each price change; the prices cannot be averaged" [@ferc2023filing, p. 26].

So the transaction-level granularity that creates the concern is not an accident of the data format. It is the deliberate product of a rulemaking in which the Commission decided that public disclosure of individual wholesale rates is what the Federal Power Act requires. I am lowering the effort needed to read data that FERC chose to publish for exactly this purpose.

The realistic effect of this project is to narrow the gap between parties who can already afford commercial services built on this data and researchers, regulators and smaller participants who cannot. I think that cuts in favor of doing it, and I would rather state the reasoning than assume it.

## The responsibility of writing a guide

PUDL has documented this dataset's structure. There is a field catalog, access instructions in four languages, a tutorial notebook, and a public list of known problems. What does not readily exist is an account of what the data means: what a row represents, that contracts are re-reported every quarter, how the two main tables relate to each other, or which fields actually hold up under use. PUDL did characterize the tables internally, but that work sits in closed issues on their tracker rather than anywhere a new user would find it, and all four tables are still labeled "experimental and/or a work in progress."

That puts this document in an awkward position. For questions about schema, a reader can check me against PUDL. For the semantic claims, which are the ones that actually determine whether an analysis is right, there is nothing to check me against. If I am wrong, a reader inherits the error with no obvious way to catch it.

I have handled this by marking uncertainty throughout. Claims I verified are stated plainly, claims I believe but have not confirmed carry a marker, and open questions are listed rather than smoothed over. Where I disagree with PUDL's documentation or FERC's own materials, I say which source I am following and why. I would rather this document be visibly incomplete than quietly wrong.

# Limitations and Future Work

## What the dataset cannot do

The most obvious gap is that the EQR has no plant identifier and no location. A
contract tells you that a company sold power and where it was delivered, but
nothing about what generated it or where that generator sits. The crosswalk in
Section 6 closes part of that gap by matching sellers to EIA utilities, which
then gives access to plant coordinates and capacity, but it reaches only 20.7%
of contract rows with fleet data attached. For the other four fifths the
question stays unanswerable with this dataset alone.

The second gap is on the buyer side. Sellers are identified by a FERC company
ID, but buyers appear only as a free-text name with no identifier of any kind.
That rules out anything that requires tracking a buyer across contracts or
across sellers, and it also means the buyer side cannot be crosswalked to EIA
the way the seller side can, since there is no stable key to anchor the match
to. Of everything missing from the EQR, this is the one I would most want back.

Price coverage is narrower than it first appears. 52.9% of contract rows carry
a rate at all, and once you require that rate to be in a single interpretable
unit, only 23.2% of transaction volume connects to a contract with a usable
price. Any study of contracted prices in the EQR is working inside that
fraction, and it is not a random fraction, since it skews toward energy and
capacity sales and away from transmission and market participation agreements.

ERCOT is effectively absent. Because most activity inside ERCOT is intrastate
and therefore outside FERC's jurisdiction over wholesale sales, Texas shows up
in the EQR only at the margins, and ERCOT does not appear anywhere in the
twenty-five largest delivery regions in Section 6. Anyone who needs ERCOT has to
go to ERCOT's own published data instead. Retail sales are out of scope
entirely for the same jurisdictional reason, so the EQR says nothing about what
end-use customers pay.

## Questions I was able to close

Two things I expected to list as limitations turned out not to be. An earlier
version of this draft stated that contracts could not be joined to transactions
and that the EQR could not be linked to other energy datasets. Section 6 shows
that both are wrong. The contract service agreement ID does link the two tables
when it is combined with the seller ID and the product name, and seller names
do match EIA utility names often enough to be useful for the subset of sellers
that own generators. I have left this paragraph in rather than quietly deleting
the old claim, because being wrong about what the data could do was itself a
consequence of there being no documentation, which is the thing this project is
about.

## What remains open

The largest unfinished piece is contract duration. The contracts table has
execution, commencement and termination dates, and a straightforward duration
calculation produced 90th-percentile contract lengths above a century while
silently dropping two thirds of the rows. That pattern almost certainly means
one or more sentinel values are being used in the date fields, but I have not
identified them, so I have left any analysis of contract length out of the
guide. Profiling the fill rates and the most common termination dates would
probably resolve it quickly, and it would unlock what I think is the single
most interesting question the EQR can answer, which is how the term structure
of wholesale contracting has changed over the thirteen years of data.

Related to that, almost everything in this guide runs on a single quarter. The
de-duplication recipe in Section 5 is demonstrated on three quarters and the
join in Section 6 on one, so none of the findings here are established as
properties of the dataset across its full span. **[TO RUN]** The 2018 Q3
version of the join is written and not yet run, and it would be the first step
toward that.

Two smaller items. I have not confirmed what negative quantities in the
transactions table actually represent, only that they are concentrated in
market settlement rows and absent from fixed-price bilateral rows. And the EIA
crosswalk stops at exact matching after normalization, so the genuine
near-misses that fuzzy matching would recover are still on the table, though
Section 6 argues that residual is small compared to the structural
non-matches.

## A regime that is closing

Everything described in this guide documents a filing regime that FERC is in
the process of replacing. On 19 March 2026 the Commission issued Order No. 917
in Docket RM23-9-000, published at 91 FR 14306 and effective 26 May 2026
[@ferc2026order917].

The headline change is a format change. The order adopts XBRL-CSV as the single
standard for EQR filing, replacing the three existing submission methods, which
are XML, CSV and manual entry through a webform. It also extends the filing
window from one month to four months after the end of the quarter, although the
Commission states that this will not take effect until the new XBRL-CSV system
is operational, and the implementation timeline itself is deferred to a future
order adopting the EQR taxonomies.

More consequential for anyone doing the kind of work in this guide, the final
rule eliminates three reporting requirements outright. Sellers will no longer
report transmission capacity reassignment information, will no longer identify
the index price publishers to which they report transactions, and will no
longer identify the exchange or broker used to consummate a transaction. The
order also adopts new data fields and clarifies the definitions of existing
ones, though the summary language does not name them.

Two of those eliminations land directly on things used in this project. PUDL's
`core_ferceqr__quarterly_index_pub` table exists to hold index publisher
reporting, so that table has an end date. And `exchange_brokerage_service` is a
column in the transactions table today that will stop being populated, which
removes the only field that says anything about how a bilateral trade was
arranged. Both are worth knowing before building anything that depends on them.

One change cuts the other way and is good news for the problem in Section 5.
The order requires refiling for up to twelve quarters when there are material
corrections or omissions, which formalizes the restatement behavior that makes
naive multi-quarter aggregation wrong. It does not remove the need to
de-duplicate, but it does put a boundary on how far back a contract can be
restated, which at least makes the problem a bounded one.

**[CHECK]** My bibliography currently cites this order as 194 FERC ¶ 61,195. I
confirmed the Federal Register citation, the docket, the effective date and the
field eliminations directly from the Federal Register text, but I could not
confirm that paragraph number, so I should either verify it against the order
itself or cite 91 FR 14306 instead.
